Representative Hasenfus, Senator Beebe-Center and esteemed members of the Joint Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety.
My name is Jason Cooney. I currently serve as a Licensing Agent and Staff

Maine, and as a private citizen. My testimony today is not representative of the
opinions or position of Maine Emergency Medical Services, the Department of
Public Safety, or the Executive Branch. I am not receiving any compensation for this testimony; it was prepared on my own time without State resources and I have
taken a personal day to be here.

LD 484 An Act Regarding the Department of Public Safety Testimony in Support March 18, 2026

Northern Light Health Government Relations 43 Whiting Hill Rd. Brewer, ME 04412

Office Main

207.973.5578 207.973.7050

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and member of the Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, my name is Lisa Harvey-McPherson RN and I am the Vice President of Government Relation for Northern Light Health. I am providing testimony today in support of this bill.
Northern Light Health organizations include 9 hospitals located in southern, central, eastern and northern Maine, nursing facilities, air and ground ambulance, behavioral health, addiction treatment, pharmacy, primary and specialty care practices and a statewide home care and hospice program. Ninety three percent of Maine's population lives in the Northern Light Health service area. Northern Light Health is also proud to be one of Maine's largest employers with more than 10,000 employees statewide.
The federal Controlled Substances Act (CSA),A created in 1970, regulates substances with abuse potential. However, it failed to address the unique needs of controlled substance use in emergency medical services (EMS) settings. This resulted in confusion and non-standard practices across states and EMS agencies. To address this challenge Congress passed the national Protecting Patient Access to Emergency Medications Act of 2017 (PPAEMA). Public Law 115-83 amends the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) to allow EMS agencies to obtain DEA registration, store medications at stations/vehicles, and use standing orders for administering, controlled substances (Schedule II-V). It enables proper care without requiring a physician's presence.
This bill is necessary to bring Maine into compliance with the federal law. We strongly support this legislation.
Thank you.

10061814:
MATTHEW RHODES Unity LD 484
Testimony in Opposition to LD 2165
Senator, Representative, and Members of the Committee,
I respectfully oppose LD 2165.
This bill does more than reorganize personnel. It quietly eliminates the independent structure of the Capitol Police and folds it into the State Police through a process of gradual replacement. Over time, the Capitol Police will no longer exist as a distinct entity.
That change deserves more scrutiny than this bill gives it.
The Capitol complex is not just another state facility. It is the seat of the legislative branch. Security in that space has traditionally been handled by a dedicated unit with a focused mission and familiarity with the unique environment of legislative operations.
LD 2165 transfers that function into the State Police chain of command, which operates under the executive branch. This creates a situation where the same branch responsible for enforcing the law is also exercising increasing control over the security environment of the Legislature.
Even if unintentional, that shift raises concerns about balance between branches of government.
The bill also relies on what is called "absorption by attrition." Rather than openly eliminating the Capitol Police, it allows the agency to disappear gradually as positions are replaced. That approach avoids a direct policy debate while still producing a permanent structural change.
If the intent is truly to eliminate the Capitol Police as a distinct entity, that proposal should be made plainly and debated on its own merits.
At a minimum, the Legislature should retain clear authority over the security of its own facilities, and any restructuring should preserve that independence rather than dilute it.
For these reasons, I urge you to vote "Ought Not to Pass."
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Respectfully submitted,
10061837:
Testimony in Support of LD 484, An Act Regarding the Department of Public Safety
Authorization to Procure, Possess, and Furnish Controlled Substances
Rick Petrie, EMT-P
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Committee:
My name is Rick Petrie, and I serve as a Paramedic with North East Mobile Health Services, providing emergency medical care across rural Maine, including some of the most remote and resource-limited communities in our state. I am here today to testify in strong support of LD 484, legislation brought forward in direct response to the federal Protecting Patient Access to Emergency Medications Act and evolving rules from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.
As a practicing paramedic, I can tell you plainly: timely access to emergency medications is not theoretical--it is the difference between life and death. In rural regions like northern Maine, EMS clinicians often operate far from hospitals, sometimes with extended transport times and limited backup. Under current and evolving federal regulatory frameworks, EMS agencies are facing increasing complexity in how controlled medications are stored, tracked, and administered in the field. While these rules are well-intentioned, without appropriate state-level alignment and support, they risk creating barriers to patient care.
LD 484 is a necessary and pragmatic response. It ensures that Maine's EMS system can remain compliant with federal law while preserving our ability to deliver critical, time-sensitive interventions. Medications such as analgesics, sedatives, and life-saving emergency drugs must be immediately available to paramedics in the field. Any delay caused by regulatory ambiguity or logistical hurdles directly impacts patient outcomes--whether that's a trauma patient in severe pain, a cardiac patient requiring rapid intervention, or a critically ill individual needing airway management.
From an operational standpoint, EMS agencies are already working diligently to maintain strict accountability, security, and documentation for controlled substances. LD 484 supports these efforts by providing clear statutory authority and alignment with federal expectations under PPAEMA. It helps eliminate uncertainty for EMS services, medical directors, and regulators, ensuring that we can continue to operate safely, legally, and effectively.
Equally important, this bill protects the sustainability of rural EMS. Agencies like ours are already facing workforce shortages, financial constraints, and increasing call volumes. Adding regulatory barriers without clear guidance or enabling legislation only compounds these challenges. LD 484 reduces administrative burden while maintaining appropriate safeguards, allowing EMS professionals to focus on what matters most--patient care.

In closing, I urge the Committee to support LD 484. This bill is about maintaining access to emergency care, supporting frontline providers, and ensuring that Maine's EMS system remains strong, compliant, and responsive to the needs of our communities.
Thank you for your time and consideration, and I am happy to answer any questions.
Respectfully submitted, Rick Petrie, EMT-P North East Mobile Health Services

Testimony of William O'Neal
Director, Maine Bureau of Emergency Medical Services (Maine EMS)
Department of Public Safety
IN SUPPORT OF LD 484
"An Act Regarding the Department of Public Safety"
Presented by Senator HASENFUS of Readfield, for Public Hearing March 18, 2026
BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON CRIMINAL JUSTICE AND PUBLIC SAFETY
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety.
My name is Wil O'Neal, and I am the Director of Maine Emergency Medical Services. I am
appearing before you today to testify in strong support of LD 484.
This legislation proposes to clarify the authority for licensed EMS agencies within the State
of Maine regarding controlled substances. Currently, Emergency Medical Services and their professionals respond to emergencies in which a controlled substance is used to treat a
life-threatening medical condition, such as a seizure. On February 5, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice's Drug Enforcement Agency released its final rule implementing EMS agency registration under the 2017 Protecting Patient Access to Emergency Medications Act, with that rule effective as of March 9, 2026. In response to this rule, Maine EMS
supports this legislation as providing needed language that directly supports our system's
provision of life-saving care.
It is worth noting that Community Paramedicine Services and Clinicians licensed bythe
Board are included in this authorization, reflecting the evolving nature of our state's healthcare delivery model.
In our other legislative efforts, we have emphasized the importance of having the right
"tools in ourtoolbox" to resolve complex regulatory circumstances. LD 484 provides similar
clarity.
Thank you for your time and for your continued support of Maine's EMS clinicians and the patients they serve. I am more than happy to participate in any work sessions regarding this bill and to answer any questions you may have.
Respectfully,
Wil O'Neal, Director, Maine EMS
